utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This morning we will hear four motions, oral arguments on four motions, first, Mr. Delic's motion for provisional release, then we will hear Mr. Delic's motion on the form of indictment, then Mr. Landzo's motion on the form of the indictment and then I understand we will go into closed session to hear Mr. Landzo's motion for provisional release. May I have appearances for counsel? For Mr. Delic? Who represents Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am Salih Karabdic, counsel assigned to the accused Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Karabdic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Appearances for Mr. Landzo, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Mustafa Brackovic, lawyer from Sarajevo, assigned to the accused Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Brackovic, are you ready to proceed for Mr. Landzo? Are you ready to go forward with these motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, your Honour, quite prepared.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances for the Prosecutor, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Good morning, I am Eric Ostberg appearing today with my co-counsel Mrs. Teresa McHenry and our case manager, Miss Elles Van Dusschoten.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, I am, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We received a request from the Prosecutor to conduct these proceedings by delayed transmission. What that means is that there will be a delay of 30 minutes for the actual transmission to go out. I have signed an order granting that request. So I wanted to tell the parties that we will be proceeding that way. The purpose is to protect and guard against any inadvertent mention of protected witnesses or persons who have asked that their names be withheld from the proceedings. We have read the papers, the motions that have been filed, and we have considered them very carefully. I have read them carefully, each of the Judges have read them carefully. So in the oral arguments today we would request that you do more than just read us back the motion that you filed, because we have already, each of us individually, read the motions. So we do not want just a repeat of what is in the motion because we have already read it. We want you to emphasis any points that you consider are particularly important, and that relates to counsel for the accused as well as the Prosecutor. We have set aside time to hear these four motions until 1.00 p.m. Today. Then, as you know, this afternoon at 2.30 we will have the status conference. So we would encourage the parties to move expeditiously so that we may hear oral arguments on the four motions and complete the oral arguments by 1.00 p.m. I have nothing else preliminarily, so why do we not proceed then with Mr. Delic's motion for provisional release? Mr. Karabdic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine, then you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: We submitted a motion for provisional release and we explained it by exceptional circumstances relating to the family circumstances of Mr. Delic. We also pointed out that Mr. Delic was ready to offer whatever guarantees might be needed that he would appear before the Court for trial, and that the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina has issued guarantees to that effect, that is, that he would be present whenever summoned by the Tribunal. The Prosecution replied to our motion with several remarks which we find unacceptable. To begin with, he said that the circumstances were in no way special. As for these extraordinary circumstances, I need to say that these provisions could not apply here and that one needs to apply general provisions from international law. I should only like to quote the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights of 1966 which says, and I shall read it in English: "It shall not be the general rule that persons awaiting trial shall be detained in custody", and so on, "but release may be subject to guarantees to appear for trial". It clearly says that one cannot stay in prison awaiting trial as a general rule, that it applies to everyone and that the release pending trial, until trial, may be conditioned only on guarantees provided that the accused will appear before the Court. A similar provision can be found in the European Convention on Political Rights, the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, which in its Article 3, Article 5, paragraph 3 says -- I shall read it in English again: "In keeping with provisions of paragraph 1, shall be entitled to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. Release may be conditioned by guarantee to appear for trial". The Rules of Proceedings and Evidence introduce a provision that any person accused before this Tribunal needs to be detained and may be released only under extraordinary circumstances. I believe that this provision of the Tribunal's Rules is a contravention of the general rules on human rights and that the provisions on human rights also apply to those accused before this Tribunal. Therefore, I believe that this provision from the Rules on the extraordinary circumstances should not be applied and that the Tribunal should apply directly these International Covenants and Conventions on the right of every man when accused to be released pending trial. Both these regulations say that a trial must be ensured and that is a condition for provisional release within a reasonable period of time. This is by no means a reasonable time. I am referring to the time since which the accused has been in prison. My client has been in prison since 2nd May when he was detained by the Bosnian court and here since 13th June. This is too long to keep him imprisoned. Moreover, it is difficult to say when the trial will start. I believe, therefore, that it is his inalienable human right to be released pending trial and he is ready to provide any guarantees needed that he will appear for trial. The second thing that the Prosecution points out is that we do not have the consent of the host country of the Netherlands government, that we do not yet know their opinion. I do not think that this Rule can stand either because the right to be released pending trial is a human right, and it cannot depend on the will of a state or state agencies or a state authority whether that person will exercise that right or not. The United Nations and the Secretary-General were bound to ensure the enforcement of rules, of regulations, on human rights for persons accused before courts and that is their right to be released pending trial, and if they fail to do so, that should in no way interfere with the right of my client to be released. I think that the provisions of these International Conventions are also binding on the Dutch government and that, in compliance with these Conventions, it should allow my client to be released to live here, to reside here, pending trial and then to appear for the trial. While respecting the orders of the Court, I shall also show which are the extraordinary circumstances. As we have already pointed out in the motions, I think that these are extraordinary circumstances indeed. In these difficult times, the man has been detained ever since 1994. It is quite evident that he has very many problems at home, and that the circumstances, his family conditions, are a great burden to him and he needs to be with his family. These are, indeed, extraordinary circumstances. It may not be so if one looks at the family circumstances of a Dutchman, say, but if we take into account the circumstances of all the Bosnians there and what we went through during these four years, it is evidently indispensable that he joins his family so as to help them, that after this frightening cataclysm that we went through in this war to help them somehow settle and start a normal life once again. This war has disrupted the lives of all of us and we need a lot of effort to settle, to calm down and start leading normal lives again; no doubt, Hazim's children and wife need this most of all in view of all the horrible things that the Bosnian people went through. Furthermore, I have also indicated other extraordinary circumstances, and that is that the mother of the accused is severely ill and that it is a question of whether she will live for much longer and that her son should be with his mother, both for his own sake and for his mother's sake. Furthermore, the accused Hazim Delic is a sick man, and I am requesting that a report be asked from the prison physician. He is suffering from various ills. He has very bad injuries in his leg, he has very bad pain in his leg, due to the herniated disc and he, by all accounts, needs an operation. He has such pain that he screams, cries out, and asks for help. According to what I have heard, he is given some drugs which seem to be narcotic drugs because he tells me that he feels as if he were flying and things like that. Therefore, I do think he should be released so he can be treated properly and so he can undergo surgery if the physicians find that it is necessary. Furthermore, the Prosecutor then referring to our motions says that we have not proven that our client will not escape, that he has been charged with very severe crimes and so on and so forth. But I should like to say that the burden of proof is not on us, and any person, and even those accused before this Tribunal, are innocent unless proved otherwise. Even though Judge Jorda confirmed the indictment against Hazim, it does not mean that Hazim is guilty. He still needs to be treated as an innocent person until sentence is passed and until that sentence becomes final. The Prosecutor may not request from us to prove that he will not escape. He is the one to show whether there are any reasons for the slightest doubt that my client intends to escape. I do not think so, and the Tribunal is trying to turn the tables on us. If the Prosecution insists on this, then I believe the Prosecution needs to prove that. I do not think there is anything to show that. The only other thing I wish to point out is that my client was not arrested, that he responded to summons, and he responded to summons and when did that without an arrest warrant he came from Orahovica to Konjic, from Konjic to Sarajevo. Only upon arriving in Sarajevo was it decided that he should be detained. Had he wanted to run, he would have done so earlier. I, therefore, believe that this cannot be attributed to him. He responded to the summons of his own free will on that occasion and he will do so if invited to appear before the Court whenever necessary. The Prosecutor says that the guarantees issued by the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina that the accused will appear for trial, rather, the Prosecutor deprecates the importance of these guarantees. I think it is offensive to our State, such an attitude, to guarantee which state recognised in this order, recognised by the international community, to belittle, to think so little of the guarantees issued by such a State. I think it is tantamount to an insult. The State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, like all other States, needs to enjoy respect and to be treated as any other State. The State of Bosnia-Herzegovina was able to bring him when the Tribunal requested that. Again it shall also be able to do so when the Tribunal requests that he appear again before Court in due time. I think the Prosecution's view that the guarantees issued by the present government may not be recognised by the government to come like seriousness. I think it is not serious. We know what the Dayton Accords are and we know that the Dayton Accords and that the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina has a continuity and has been recognised since April 1992, and that it shall also maintain its legal sovereignty and its legal person even after the elections. Of course, some authorities may change, but these authorities recognise and must recognise, they must assume and will assume, by Dayton Accord all the commitments of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina had assumed in the period before these elections. That would be all that I would have to say. I wish to draw to a close and say that, as has been said, my client's motion is justified and that he should be released. We now leave it to the Court to determine whether these guarantees suffice or whether additional guarantees are needed. We are ready to do all within our power, but we do not think that this is necessary and that what we have supplied so far is quite enough. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Who will respond for the Prosecution? Ms McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will. Your Honours, I would just like to briefly respond to some of the points raised by the Defence in their argument. With respect to the remainder, we will rely on our prior papers. The first thing is that the Statute of this Tribunal and the Rules have a presumption that someone will be detained. It is the accused's burden to overcome that presumption. That presumption in the Tribunal's Rules and Statute are in full conformity with international standards in so far, in this case, as very specific, well founded and essential reasons for the detention exist, thus justifying release only in exceptional circumstances. Here the accused has not been able to meet any of the requirements set out in our Rules. The only argument put forward in the written papers of the accused has to do with the accused's family. Given that every accused has family, we do not believe that this can in any way be considered exceptional. With respect to some of the other things the Defence said today, to the extent that the accused has been incarcerated for most of the time since 1994, it is not because of this Tribunal's proceedings; it is because in his own country he was convicted of murder and was serving a sentence for which he eventually was released pursuant to, I believe, a general amnesty. With respect to the medical circumstances of the accused, this is the first that the Prosecution has heard about these. We know that the Registrar is in charge of the accused's medical care. We would just respectfully suggest that if the Defence wants to follow this up, they ask for a written report from the Registrar from an appropriate medical practitioner about the exact situation. But certainly there is nothing in this record which would demonstrate exceptional circumstances that would justify any kind of release. With respect to the question, will the accused appear for trial, we note that there are no specific practical measures proposed that would provide any kind of assurance that this accused would appear. This is again not acceptable. We will note that the accused did not turn himself into the authorities after the arrest warrant was returned, despite the wide publicity, especially in this area, given to the indictment and the arrest warrants. Apparently, eventually, after some six weeks or so when the authorities made some effort to get him -- I do not know the full circumstances, but at least after some period of time they did gain custody of him. After being taken into custody, the accused fought his extradition to The Hague, including appealing to the Supreme Court. Now that he has been here and has seen some of the evidence against him, we suggest that there is even an increased risk of flight. With respect to the assertion that Bosnia will ensure that the accused is available to the Tribunal, as we have stated many times, the Tribunal is very grateful for Bosnia's co-operation with the Tribunal. Certainly our suggestion that the guarantee is not sufficient is not any sort of insult or anything else to them. But it must be noted that it appears that the report is that they will comply with their legal obligations to turn over the accused if they are able to find the accused in his home. There are no assurances, however, regarding how Bosnia or even this Tribunal could be assured that the accused would, in fact, remain in his house. Further, we note that there are a number of outstanding issues regarding Bosnia's ability to turn over the accused. These issues are complicated by the new political structures after Dayton and after the recent elections. Thus, with all due respect, we believe that before this Chamber would rely on the document issued by Bosnia, an official representative of the Bosnian government should be asked to speak on the record regarding the assurances that they are able to give. The Bosnian representative could be heard in official court session, thereby assuring all parties are aware of the facts relied upon, assuring that the parties have an opportunity to explore relevant issues and, finally, ensuring that a full record exists in the event of a subsequent appeal or later problems about what was agreed to. With respect, finally, to the question of whether the accused would pose a danger to victims and witnesses, the Prosecution would first point to the allegations in the indictment which detail an horrific set of crimes, including the accused's personal participation in murder, torture and rape. These allegations alone should be sufficient to indicate that the accused poses a danger to victims and witnesses. In addition to those allegations, we note, among other things, that the accused is a convicted murderer in his own country, that no specific protections regarding his movements are offered, and that the accused is aware of the identity of a number of victims and potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We received or, at least, I received a guarantee this morning. I suppose we can ask Mr. Karabdic some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have listened to your oral presentation. As I indicated, we did read the papers. Judge Stephen, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I did have a question to ask of Defence counsel: Looking at the guarantee, I see on the second page, the second last paragraph of the guarantee does not make sense in the English language. It refers to the delegation of Esad Landzo, that he will up to the determination of the procedure before the Tribunal stay in his house. Am I right in understanding the word "delegation" is intended to mean the agreement or promise of Landzo to stay in his house?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I must say that I gave the original to the Tribunal, I have given the original to the Tribunal, but it certainly means yes, the undertaking. But let me say something in connection with what the Prosecutor's counsel has said, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps before you do that, if you could clearly answer the question? "Delegation" is to be understood by us as the promise or undertaking so that the guarantee is conditional on the undertaking of your client to stay in his house, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I think that we speak about both the promise and the obligation on my client to stay in his house and the obligation of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it will make sure that he stays in his house and that it will pay attention to the fact that he must come to the Tribunal when summoned. If necessary, I can perhaps translate because I have not got the original Bosnian text with me, but I can perhaps interpret it from the English text? Probably the translation was wrong and the official translator might have been using the terms which are not the best in the legal terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is the second last paragraph, if you would turn to it? Do you see the second last paragraph? It begins "This guarantee has the full validity".

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: "This guarantee", yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then it goes on ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I will read to you the Bosnian original and it will be interpreted: "This guarantee has the full validity if the International Tribunal decides to temporarily, provisionally release Esad Landzo and makes it possible for him to defend himself from freedom with this statement" -- there is a misprint here, there seems to be a misprint -- "given the undertaking of Hazim Delic that until the end of the Tribunal proceedings it will stay in his house". This is the first time we said "Esad Landzo" and it should actually stand not "Esad Landzo" but "Hazim Delic". So that Hazim Delic should be temporarily released and defend himself from the state of freedom with his undertaking that until the end of the proceedings he will be staying in his house at Orahovica, a community of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: It was a misprint, but the meaning, what is meant, I think, is very clear.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So Mr. Delic has undertaken then to remain in his house?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes. If the Tribunal, Trial Chamber, allows him. If there are any other conditions, if he should be staying in Holland, he is prepared to stay in Holland.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But the undertaking then of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that not conditioned on Mr. Delic remaining in his house? By that I mean if for some reason he does not remain in his house, then what is the obligation then of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina will take all the necessary steps to make sure that he stays in his house, in his village. It will take care to see to it that he does not leave the house. That is the obligation of the Bosnian State and it is the obligation on Mr. Delic that he has undertaken that he would not leave his house and his village. That is what he is undertaking to do. The State of Bosnia-Herzegovina will monitor the situation and will, of course, see to it that this undertaking is met. I think it is the usual practice that if somebody has been accused or indicted and has been temporarily released, the authorities will always watch over him to make sure that he stays where he is obliged to stay or that he reports to the police authorities or that the authorities inspect the way that he behaves and what he does and so on. This is the substance of the undertaking of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this undertaking, I think, is a serious one, needs to be taken seriously, and both important and sufficient guarantee that this will be the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does the guarantee provide that Bosnia-Herzegovina will be responsible for Mr. Delic remaining in his house? Is that how you read the undertaking or the guarantee, rather?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I interpret the guarantee to mean that Bosnia-Herzegovina will take all the necessary steps in its power to make sure that Mr. Delic is in his house, and that the State will take everything necessary, all necessary steps to prevent his flight. But, obviously, he can move around the house and in the village, but he could not travel, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that stated specifically in the guarantee because I do not see any language that would support that position? Is that said in the guarantee either in Bosnian or in English, or is that your interpretation of the guarantee?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I think it follows logically from the text of the guarantee but, if necessary, we can probably obtain further undertakings or further explanations of what is meant, but that is how I understand, how I read the guarantee, and I think everybody should read it in that same spirit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, would you like to respond to the guarantee issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Not only did we read the guarantee to say that Bosnia's assurance that the accused would appear was premised on the accused's undertaking that he would remain in his house, to the extent that the Office of the Prosecutor has had prior conversations with Madam Vidovic, the official representative of the Bosnian government, when a similar issue was raised with another accused, our understanding is that Bosnia is not able to guarantee that the accused will stay in his house and they do not mean to imply that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know whether it is appropriate for the Trial Chamber to consider anything regarding the guarantee other than what is written in the guarantee. We have the guarantee in Bosnian and in English. So we will read it and apply our understanding of it. I have just a couple of questions, sir, of you: Mr. Karabdic. Rule 65 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence provide that, "Once detained, an accused may not be released except upon an order of a Trial Chamber". That is sub-section (A). Subsection (B) provides, "Release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only in exceptional circumstances, after hearing the host country and only if it is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial and, if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person". You have indicated in your argument that international standards provide that detention should be the exception rather than the rule, and that if our Rules provide for the contrary, then our Rules are in derogation of international standards. So my question to you is, has not the European Court of Human Rights in applying the international standards held that you look to the type of crime that the accused is charged with in making this determination? So, is it not relevant, considering that our Tribunal is charged with trying persons who have been charged with the commission of serious violations of International Humanitarian Law -- in this instance, murder, rape, conditions of confinement at the detention, a number of charges that are in the indictment -- for our Tribunal in determining whether or not an accused should be released, is it not relevant for us to look to the type of offence charged and would that not comport with decisions of the European Court of Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I think that the international provisions of the international law are very clear and they make no exception as to the right of the detained person to be released and to defend himself from freedom. The rules apply, I believe, also for those who stand indicted before this Trial Chamber. The danger for the victims, the danger for the witnesses and for other persons does not exist. There is no danger. The Prosecution has not given any indication or any suspicion as to this kind of danger. The witnesses are scattered all over the place, throughout the world. They are not in Orahovica. There no witnesses in Orahovica on whose statements the Prosecution relies or the indictment relies. The accused has not shown in any way with his behaviour that he might represent a danger for anybody or to anybody. I, therefore, think that there is no reason for his further detention. It is my firm belief that there are no and there can be no exceptions to the implementation of the rules of international law on release from detention. Neither this Trial Chamber nor the accused before this Trial Chamber can be treated as an exception. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The indictment charges that Mr. Delic was Deputy Commander of the Celebici camp. In the indictment he is charged with the commission of several murders, beatings and other acts which are serious charges at least, and most definitely he is innocent until the Prosecutor proves that he is guilty of each of the counts beyond a reasonable doubt, but my questioning is not focusing on the danger to the victims, potential danger or the alleged danger to the victims and witnesses, but on the nature of the charges, and has not the European Court of Human Rights held that it is permissible and appropriate to look at the nature of the charge? A person charged with pickpocketing, for example -- to use an extreme example -- might be treated differently than a person who is charged with the commission of several violations, serious violations, of International Humanitarian Law. I think you tell me, no. You tell me it does not make any difference, but you correct me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: There is a difference, of course, but I would like to reiterate that the international rules and laws apply also to people who stand accused before this Tribunal. Whether they are guilty or not will be found later in the actual trial. I do not have the decision that you are referring to and I cannot consult it now, but I have here the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the European Charter. I think that they do not give the Court the right to detain people in prison simply because they have been indicted, simply because there is an indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you believe that the unique circumstances of this Tribunal is a relevant consideration in determining whether or not exceptional circumstances exist? By that I mean this Tribunal has no police force. We are sitting in The Hague thousands of miles away from the place where the accused will be. We, the Tribunal, has faced enormous -- that is probably not even the appropriate word because it is more serious -- obstacles from countries because they have failed to execute the arrest warrant. So that although we have issued, I do not know, 70 some indictments, the Prosecutor has issued 70 some indictments, after being confirmed by one of the Judges, several countries have ignored their obligation under international law to execute those arrest warrants and we have no police power. Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you have indicated, is in a different situation. They have co-operated in this instance. But, keeping in mind again the guarantee, do you not think that that is a factor that makes our Rules, the Tribunal's Rules, a little different than those that might apply in a national country where the accused is within the borders of the country and there is a police force?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: These are problems, of course, that need to be resolved, but they ought to be resolved by those who established this Court and this Tribunal. This question cannot be settled at the expense of the accused, of people who have been brought here before this Trial Chamber. I think that no special rights, no greater rights, appertain to this Tribunal compared to any other Tribunal or any other court. A great deal ought to be discussed about the attitude of the founders of this Tribunal towards the Tribunal. Unfortunately, those who killed almost 300,000 Bosnian people, they are not here in this Trial Chamber, but we have some poor people from another nation who are responsible or held responsible for a few acts simply because the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina is co-operative. While we have very well documented and proved crimes of thousands of people being killed and massacred, these perpetrators are not here because of the political reason and because of the inactivity of the founders of this Tribunal and of the super powers or powers that were involved in its establishment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question about Mr. Delic's health? Do you have a report from his physician regarding the status of his health? That is the first question. The second question is, based on your representations, it may be appropriate, if it is possible, for the Registry to request a physician to examine Mr. Delic and submit a report to the Trial Chamber. Would that be permissible with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I agree with this proposal, this last proposal, but I have direct contact with the accused and from him I learn that he was ill. I was also informed by the prison management. They told me that he is suffering pain, that he has been asking for a doctor. Also, I have had information from his family with whom he talks over the telephone. He complains of pain and suffering and, obviously, he would not be telling his family unless it was a very serious kind of pain and illness. As far as I can judge, some medical examinations have been undertaken. A specialist has examined him. I also agree with your suggestion that the Trial Chamber should, perhaps, ask for a medical opinion of the prison medical service. I am sure that that examination will prove, quite clearly, that his health is seriously deteriorating, and that this is just another reason for him to be temporarily released.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I understand from the papers that have been submitted, Mr. Delic was convicted by a military court in Bosnia-Herzegovina and sentenced to, was it 15 years or 10 years, for murder? Is that a relevant consideration for the Trial Chamber in deciding whether or not it considers that Mr. Delic will be a danger to victims and witnesses? I may be wrong about the terms. It may have been 10 years. I really do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Nine years. Nine years was the sentence, but it had been reduced on several occasions. Mr. Delic was released from the serving of this sentence, which means that the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina decided that he represented no danger to the State, to the community, and that he may be free. I think that this is something which we also need to take into account and respect.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that the general amnesty that all convicted persons received or was this something that was directed specifically at Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: All of these decisions were made for Mr. Delic specifically and in these decisions there were some other people involved, but he was mentioned by name in these decisions. So, first of all, the sentence was reduced, reduced on several occasions, and eventually he was released. He was actually released before he had served the full sentence term.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else on this motion for the accused or for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to raise one other matter. There was a motion that was filed on September 26th. It was a motion seeking leave for an additional filing. Does that relate to the form of the indictment? It does. OK. We will talk about that then when we get to it. The next motion that we wish to consider is Mr. Delic's motion on the form of the indictment. Would you proceed, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: If I may, I should like my colleague to continue on the same subject, that is in prison, but I may go on, if you like.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not have a preference. You can talk among you and then we could present -- we could hear .....

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: All right, I shall proceed. May I?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not have a preference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel please switch on the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague thought that I should also be speaking about the provisional release, but you said that we would be discussing it this afternoon in camera, so I just explained to my colleague how were things. It is all right, I accept it, and I shall, therefore, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We were going to discuss it in camera, as I understand it, at the preference of the accused, is that correct? Not this afternoon, no, this morning, I meant that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in closed session. In any event, perhaps I did not quite get you, whether it would be in the afternoon. But, whatever the case, the request was to do it in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good thank you. Then, Mr. Karabdic, it looks like you have to go first again and this time on Mr. Delic's motion on the form of the indictment. Again we have read the papers. Your argument on the motion for provisional release, I think, was very succinct and to the point and hit the major points persuasively. If you approach this motion the same way, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall need some more time now and I should like to apologise in advance. When we arrived here to defend, both I and my fellow lawyer and other colleagues from Bosnia, I must say that we were rather taken by surprise when we saw what an indictment before this Court looked like, and that it read counter to some of the ideas that we had before that. I should like to say here that Bosnia is a part of Europe; that in Bosnia we have the European system of criminal proceedings and such a European system has been there in force for over 120 years; that we have quite a long standing experience; that the European criminal procedure was introduced in our land by Austria Hungary which was a rule of law and order, as everybody knows, and did its utmost to see those European standards and rules introduced in Bosnia. So they were and they still are there in force with, perhaps, some slight modifications. However, here we came across an indictment which looks quite differently from what we are used to. When we made our objections and motions in this regard, we were always responded that it was a common law system, Anglo Saxon system, and the like. However, personally, I do not think that that is the case because neither the Statute nor the Rules determine that what is called common law ought to be applied in the proceedings. I think that the manner in which these indictments are drawn up is in contravention of the recognised civilisation norms of criminal procedure. We do believe this to be indeed the case. I shall be able to reason this out. Secondly, whenever we made a motion, whenever we had some objection, the Prosecution bombarded us with some decisions and rulings passed in Tadic's case, for instance, or when it comes to motions regarding the accused Mucic, which I simply think to be erroneous. We do not know under which circumstances those decisions were taken. I do not think we can discuss them before this Court. What is even more important, even if these decisions were all right and everything, they cannot be used as precedents in this particular case and what we are advocating before this Court, because neither the Statute nor the Rules have a provision saying that earlier decisions of the Court were binding on the Court or, rather, on the Tribunal with regard to the future decisions, that is, that the Court should be bound by its earlier decisions in some cases yet to come. This is not either the Statute or the Rules. Therefore, I am not going to touch upon all those decisions or all those quotations which the Prosecution has served on us. Thirdly, another thing which came as a surprise to me was the following. The indictment was filed. I also filed motions. The Prosecution replied to these motions. When I studied those motions, I deemed it necessary to respond to them in writing and to express my views in writing. I did so. I think I am entitled to do it in that way under Rule 72 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. However, a couple of days ago I received from the Registrar a letter saying that I had not asked for the permission of the Court to submit my response to the Prosecutor's response, and that I should ask for it. I did not have this response and I had only a couple of days at my disposal. So I wrote it the best I could on the basis of that information received from the Deputy Registrar. When I arrived here, I was served the decision of the Chamber of, I believe, 16th May 1996, which determines that whenever a party submits a brief or a motion the other party has the right to respond to it. If one wishes to continue writing and submitting this, then an additional permission of the Court needs to be sought. But ever since we had been assigned the counsel for these accused, nobody informed us about this and nor did we know about this decision. However, when I an analysed this decision I saw that it referred to Article 54 or to Rule 54. However, this Rule refers to specific orders, rather than general rules of procedure, that is, orders in some specific cases. However, a Chamber issues a rule of procedure, but I do not think that a Chamber may do that. It is only all the Judges of this Tribunal who may do so under Article 15 of the Statute. So that I do not know whether my response was accepted, whether it is before the Chamber and whether it will be taken note of. Furthermore, as regards the form of the indictment, there is a provision under Article 84 which says that in English about crimes with which the accused is charged under the Statute. The Tribunal was due to develop this rule further, that is, this rule under Rule 15 and how to apply it. However, as this statutory rule is explained in Rule 47(B), to my mind, differs from the Statute and only confuses the issue. I, therefore, think that the provision under 47(B) is inapplicable. I think it ought to be ignored because what it prescribes is something completely different from what the Statute says. Here we have something of the case and this has no bearing whatsoever, nor does it explain what it refers to, I mean facts of the case, we do not know what that is, because the case is a broad one and it is not clear what it refers to. Then it also says a concise statement, a concise statement that it refers both to the facts of the case and of the crime and the criminal offence which is not true, according to the Statute. The most important thing is that it completely ignores the statutory provision that the indictment must say that somebody is indicted under this Statute. In the Rules there is nothing about that. The Rules abolish this. I, therefore, think that what these Rules do is confuse the issues and make it more difficult to apply the Statute. I thus think this Rule ought to be disregarded. In my view, as specified by the Statute and the indictment, must include facts, that is the facts which mean full description of the offence, the means of perpetration, the manner of the perpetration of the offence, the facts thereof, so that one can, indeed, conclude that a crime as specified by Statute has been committed. I believe that other counsel for the Defence have also moved in this direction, but the Prosecutor somehow tried to evade a response to it in two ways. First, the Prosecution referred to the Article which speaks about the rights of the accused, that he needs to be notified of the nature of the indictment and so on and so forth, which is something completely else, which talks about the human rights and so on and so forth, rather than an act, a procedural act, such as indictment. Secondly, the Prosecution also tried to avoid this issue by saying that the particulars ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can interrupt you for a moment? I do not follow what you are saying about the inconsistency between the Rules and the Statute because I look at Article 18.4 of the Statute and it seems to be word for word the same as Rule 47(B), containing "a concise statement of the facts and the crime or crimes with which the accused is charged under the Statute". I read the Statute. I then look at 47(B) which you attack and it says, "... a concise statement of the facts of the case and of the crime with which the suspect is charged". What is the point you are making?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not clear enough, but the facts and words are completely different and Article 18.4 and Rule 47(B) sound differently. In 47(B) there is another added word which is "of the case" which is not clear and which says nothing. There is also an "and" added. As it is worded here, what derives from it is that the concise statement relates both to the facts and the crime, that the concise statement also relates to the crime. That is according to the Rules. The Rules also do not have this wording under the Statute. To my mind, this is of paramount importance.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand your position, but 47(B) says, "... concise statement of the facts of the case", and you are correct that is not in 18.4, but then it goes on to say, "and of the crime with which the suspect is charged". Of course, 18.4 does say "crime". It also says "facts". Your position is that the words "of the case" is something new that is in 47(B) that is not in 18.4. You are correct. If I were to read that, I would -- well, maybe I should not make a judgment so quickly, it seems to be broader, that is, 47(B) may place a greater obligation on the Prosecutor than 18.4 in the Statute, because it makes them give a concise statement of the facts of the case and of the crime; whereas 18.4 just says "a concise statement of the facts and the crime or crimes". But I guess your position is that to the extent that the Trial Chamber relies on 14(B) and 14(B) places a lesser obligation on the Prosecution, then that is ultra vires, or 47(B) is because it contradicts the Statute. So the question is whether 47(B) places a lesser requirement on the Prosecutor in terms of what it must allege in the indictment and whether the Trial Chamber is accepting that lesser standard, if there is one, in 47(B) as opposed to 18.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I think that the Statute enjoys primacy and that the Tribunal ought to apply the Statute, and the Statute says that the indictment must follow the Statute. I think that a concise statement, at least as one reads the Statute, pertains only to the facts, nothing else. When one reads the Rules, the concise statement refers also to the crime, not to mention that it disregards a specific provision of the Statute that the indictment must follow the Statute, that is, that the indictment must make reference to the Statute. In my view and on the basis of legal practice and the standards applied in the civilised world, the indictment in its factual part must contain a full description of the crime, and in the part about the crime it must contain the definition and description of the crime under the Statute or, rather, under international treaty in this particular case. I can explicitly say that the Prosecutor did not abide by this Rule. But I also wish to say another thing -- I have tried to do that and your Honour interrupted me -- that the Prosecution tried to avoid answering when counsel for the Defence requested that the facts, that the particulars in the indictment, be indicated. The Prosecution avoided it and replied that the particulars are in the supporting material. I think that such reply is unacceptable and needs to be rejected. To begin with, this Statute makes no mention of supporting material whatsoever. Therefore, when the Statute speaks about the form of the indictment, it did not bear this in mind. A indictment needs to be complete, that is, contain a full description of a crime, of a felony, independently and supporting material which the Rules introduced may only be used to corroborate as a proof of what the indictment says, rather than a supplement to the indictment, because we cannot defend our clients from the supporting material. We can only defend them on the basis of the indictment. The Prosecutor must say what transpires from this material and then bring charges. Only then when this is in the indictment can we defend our clients. We cannot defend them on the basis and against supporting material. I, therefore, opine that this Prosecution's reasoning cannot be accepted. Furthermore, I also said that in my written briefs, and I am not going to repeat that, but nevertheless the indictment lacks precision. Often times, legal terms are used in factual descriptions, rather than say X and Y have perpetrated this or that, legal terms are used, and their factual descriptions, they are only references to the conditions and, therefore, the indictment is not precise. Legal questions arising with regard to this indictment: The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia under Article 1, under Article 1 of the Statute, was established to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. In other words, every crime and every count of the indictment must be accompanied by statements saying which provision of international law has been violated, because that is the right of every accused. I can refer here to the International Covenant on Human Rights. I read it: "No-one shall be accused for crimes which were not crimes under domestic or international law at the moment of their perpetration, nor can a sentence be pronounced", etc., etc. I am not going to read any further. This is Article 15. The Prosecutor has many counts and where he only refers to a provision of the Statute, but the Statute does not prescribe criminal responsibility. All the Statute does is pronounce the competence of the Tribunal. The Statute relates to the procedural rather than to substantive law. The Statute says that somebody may be brought for trial if he committed a serious violation of International Humanitarian Law and so on and so forth, but were summoned to be brought for trial in addition to statutory provisions, one must also make reference to provisions of international law which were violated, because so and so only may the competence of this Tribunal be placed on solid grounds. I realised in time that my motion was a motion relative to the competence of the Tribunal because the Prosecution did not offer evidence, nor did they indicate the grounds on the basis of which this Tribunal should act upon, that is, the Tribunal can act only if somebody is accused for serious violations of international law, and in more than half of the counts the Prosecution only refers to the Statute which, to my mind, is impermissible. When I made my motions, I indicated this to the Prosecution and the Prosecution admits that that is so, but does nothing and still insists that is a proper form of the indictment and this is the indictment with which one has to go for the trial. I mean, he does nothing. He recognises that this is not right and yet proceeds to do as before, and this cannot be done. This is not done. I am sorry. Excuse me for a moment. Secondly, the Prosecutor has several counts which I think are quite groundless. He charges a man for the violation of the Statute as one count and, as another count, severe violation, grave breach of the Geneva Conventions are committed in law, all violations of laws and customs of war. When this is objected to, then he says he can be sentenced twice for these things, but I do not think that this can hold water and it cannot do so, because we are talking about one crime and not two counts, anything that this issue needs to be resolved in the pretrial proceedings. Perhaps I may have omitted some of the arguments but they can be found in my written brief. I wish to point out one more thing and that relates to the background to the basic data. In the indictment the Prosecutor proceeds as if in this case this was an inter-ethnic conflict, and as though Bosnian Croats and Muslims had attacked Bosnian Serbs, that is, he draws a sign of equality between the conduct of all parties, that is, implying that all sides were the same and so on and so forth, and disregards an important, if not a fundamental, fact which is common knowledge, that the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established under the forces which held that those villages indicated in the indictment were the rebel forces, that they were not regular forces, that they were the forces which served the attack on Bosnia-Herzegovina; and that by that very effect Bosnia-Herzegovina was entitled to undertake any possible measures against such people. It was indispensable because those forces held Bradina and Donje Selo. Bradina in the north and Donje Selo in the south. Konjic was so blocked that there was no way through. All the communications with the rest of us is Herzegovina were cut. It is evident, and the State is authorised and the forces loyal to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had all the right to occupy and to liberate those areas. It was the liberation of one's own territory. Persons who did that, who kept that, were not civilians. They may have worn civilian clothes, but they all wore arms and they all fought against Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is said even by the witnesses whom the Prosecution intends to call, not to mention a case when a man says, "I came to visit my mother-in-law. It was on the eve of the war. I came to pay her a visit and I was given an automatic", somebody gave him. So everybody was armed, because the JNA armed those people and they were in the service of an outside enemy, of an external enemy, and the State had to act against them. When eventually the State came to that territory and the forces loyal to it, then this State had the right to detain them, to arrest them, under all rules, under its domestic rules, as rebels, as perpetrators, as persons who were in possession of weapons contrary to its stipulations and also under international rules they may not enjoy protection as civilians. Therefore, these provisions in the background or, rather, the background needs to be changed. We cannot accept that. Towards the end, there is a special paragraph which speaks about unlawful imprisonment of civilians because this detention was lawful. They plied their weapons, they attacked. Had it not been done, then the fate of Konjic would have been the same as the fate of Kozarac or Prijedor and other places where well-known tragedies happened which we need not talk about again here. That will be that. I have said a great deal about the form of the indictment, but how does it reflect on the indictment against Mr. Delic, against Mr. Hazim Delic? All I can say is that Delic is accused as Deputy Commander of the camp without any proof whatsoever. I have seen no evidence that he had ever been appointed or anything like it. Secondly, I have seen nothing about why a Deputy Commander should be responsible for what the Commander is responsible for. A Commander is a superior person, so I do not see why a Deputy Commander should be held responsible for it. I cannot see that anywhere and it does not transpire from the indictment. Furthermore, I can also say that my client is in a very odd situation. He has been charged twice for one and the same crime. First, there are paragraphs which say that he participated in this or that, and then this and that died. Later on it says, as a superior, he is responsible for that same crime. I think that this nightmare, that one cannot do it that way. In line with what I said before about the indictment, Hazim Delic needs to be clearly said what he is charged for as an immediate perpetrator, and that is what we will then defend against. He must also be clearly said what crimes were perpetrated by others and on what grounds is he being held responsible for those acts committed by others. In other words, each one of the counts of the indictment where he is charged for crimes perpetrated by others needs to contain all the ingredients for the crimes of others, plus the facts which will indicate his responsibility for those crimes committed by others and also under which Rule, under which Article, is he being charged. I think that this indictment cannot be accepted and one cannot proceed on the basis thereof, that it needs to be returned to the Prosecution for amendment. If the Prosecution insists on this indictment, then it has to be rejected. Just a moment, please. The separation of accusations is necessary to make a defence possible at all. We do not know what Delic is accused of. All the points in the indictment are such that we cannot respond to them. We cannot defend the accused against them. Therefore, I think that the indictment should be made clearer by separating the charges and only then can Mr. Delic properly defend himself and can actually participate in the proceedings. Let me add also that in making my motions, preliminary motions, I objected to the form of the indictment, but actually my objections are also objections to the competence of this Court. I am not questioning or denying the competence of the Court, but there is no basis in the indictment for making this Court competent to hear this indictment. I, therefore, would now move and add to what I said earlier, namely, first, that the indictment should be rejected practically in all its points and counts because the defects and flaws are present at almost every step in the indictment. Alternatively, the indictment could be sent back to the Prosecutor to remove the defects within a reasonable period of time. I apologise, your Honours, for speaking for so long. I may have also missed some of the things which I wanted to say, but I am prepared to give further explanations if needed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The motion seeking leave for additional filing was filed on September 26th. That is the motion that you wanted to file as a reply to the Prosecutor's motion -- as a reply to the Prosecutor's response. This Trial Chamber has entered a standing order which says that all responses are to be filed within 14 days of a filing of a motion. So a motion is filed and then the standing order says responses are to be filed within 14 days. There is no provision in that standing order for the filing of a reply. That is why it was sent back because there is no provision for the filing of a reply. But all we were asking was that a motion for leave to file this reply be filed and that you did. In the reply that you filed, however, to the extent that you are raising jurisdictional issues which were not raised in your first motion, it may not be timely but that is something, I suppose, we can talk about when we return. As to the competence of the Tribunal and the subject matter jurisdiction, over the recess, if you wish, look at the Secretary-General's Report, paragraphs 33 through 36. It seems to me that what the Secretary-General is saying is that the Statute that was drafted incorporates both conventional law and customary international law. To the extent that the subject matter jurisdiction is based on conventional international law, it is only that that has become a part of customary international law. But look at those paragraphs and see if that responds to you because I would like to discuss it. But we will stand in recess for 20 minutes. When we return, we will hear from the Prosecutor. We will then proceed and then hear, perhaps, from the accused again and perhaps again from the Prosecutor and then proceed on Mr. Landzo's motion on the form of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, will you respond to ----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will do that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karabdic, indeed, has a broad approach in attacking the form of the indictment, starting with a history of European standards and questioning the foundation in the Statute of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, and going so far as to trying to convince the Trial Chamber to disregard or ignore Rule 47 in which I do not think he will succeed. He is also raising a lot of fundamental legal issues, such as existing international law of which Madam President already briefly dealt or just underlined, to put the submission of the Prosecutor on the record, that the Security Council did not legislate in instituting this International Tribunal, but relied on existing international law. At the end of what Mr. Karabdic said, he said something of the competence of the Tribunal which I really did not understand. Maybe we will have some clarification as to what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think what he said is that the Covenant, Article 15, International Covenant, speaks to -- I guess it will be an ex post facto claim, then that our Statute prohibits that, trying of persons if it will result in ex post facto -- trying of persons for violations of laws that did not exist at the time that they committed the offence. He says that what the Statute has done is to create these crimes. That is how I understood his argument, however. So what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will rely, of course, on our written response to Mr. Delic's motions and highlight some of the questions. This Chamber has already many times dealt with the meaning of the words "concise statement of the facts of the case". In our written response, we have quoted your Honours' decision on the motion of the co-accused Mucic on the same matter. I do not think that you would like me to read it here and now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may read the applicable portion, not the whole decision, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This is in our response quoted from case No. IT-96-21-T, decision on the accused Mucic's motions for particulars. "The place, the approximate date and the names of the alleged victims are provided. On the issue of the involvement of the accused, the Prosecution asserts that in this case Mucic was the Commander of the Celebici camp and, therefore, had command responsibility", etc. "The direct responsibility charges relate to a prolonged course of conduct. For instance, the inhumane conditions at the camp, the unlawful confinement of the civilians and the plunder of property. "The factual allegations underlying these charges indicate the approximate time period during which the conduct occurred, describe the underlying conduct with specificity and provides some information about the participation of the accused and others." This is, in the estimation of the Court, giving him a warning of the nature of the crimes with which he is charged and sets out the factual basis of the charges. That, I believe, we have done even in this case. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the indictment now in question is in compliance with the Statute and the Rules and also with the just read statement of this Trial Chamber. Many other questions were raised. I will turn to the questions of cumulative charging adopted by the Office of the Prosecutor. This manner of charging is somewhat unfamiliar, even to me, but it certainly does not mean that the defendant is accused of more than one criminal act. It just means that this act is falling under more than one of the Articles of our Statute. This Chamber has already this time in the Tadic case ruled -- I will just briefly quote -- "What is to be punished is proven criminal conduct and that will not depend on technicalities of pleading". Consequently, this problem will be taken care of when we reach the stage of sentencing. At the end of Mr. Karabdic's oral statement here today, he challenged the correctness of the description of the underlying conflict in which the alleged crimes took place. He contends, as far as I can understand, that the Bosnian forces had the right to attack and imprison the Serbs and the Croats in the villages. However, the issue is not why a conflict erupted. The issue is whether in that conflict International Humanitarian Law was violated. That is what this indictment is all about. Mr. Karabdic also took up the question whether Delic was or was not a Deputy Commander and his superior authority in the prison camp in the Celebici camp. This is, in our submission, a matter of fact and the validity of that fact must be proven at trial and not at this point of time. I will see if I have something more on what we have listened to. I think, your Honours, this is what I find necessary to say in response to what we have heard from Mr. Karabdic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Karabdic, as I recall, alleged that the indictment was not sufficient because, although perhaps under common law system the pleading would be sufficient, Bosnia is a part of the civil law system, has been a part of Europe for a long time, and there is nothing in the Statute that requires the common law system of pleading be adopted. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It is an interesting question, how much of common law and civil law, who have been the fathers of writing this Statute and adopting these Rules. I see ingredients from both these legal systems and I do not think this is a valid way of questioning the indictment, saying that it is not in the parameters of one or another of these systems. The issue is: is it in the parameters of our Statute and our Rules on procedure? That is my submission, that it is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 18.4, I think it is, lays down at least from the Statute the requirement -- yes, 18.4 -- and so I think that Mr. Karabdic would say: "Well, that may be true, but then when you get to 47(B) there is a different standard".

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is your position regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: As far as I understand from Mr. Karabdic, the reason of the inconsistency should be based on the fact that the word "the case" is not to be found in 18.4 but is found in 47(B).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there a difference? Is there a significant difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In my view, there is no difference. I do not think this diminishes or makes greater any of the rights to indict the way we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Wasn’t there one other point made, that the word "of" appears in 47(B) and "of the crime", so it is a concise statement "of the crime" in 47(B) which does not appear in the Statute and, therefore, "concise statement" only governs what has to appear in the indictment, according to 47 and not according to the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have never made any distinction at all, your Honour, in respect of these two ways of putting it. I really find it hard to see any difference. I found 47 well founded in the Article.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Karabdic also says that your citings to the Tadic decision, decisions from the Tadic case, are inappropriate because they are not binding precedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK. I noted that and I forgot to say something about it. Of course, there is nothing saying that any Chamber is bound by what another Chamber did, or not even that any Chamber is bound what the Appeals Chamber said, etc. But it is certainly to be considered, as any type of law I am familiar with, as valid guidelines and for the consistency of the way this Tribunal in these different Chambers are dealing, of course, to rely on what has happened before, taking guidance from what has been done in the other Chamber or in previous cases. That is exactly what the Prosecutor does. We read, of course, what happens in the Tadic case and the rulings of this and other Chambers. We take that as guidelines without finding us either bound by it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Karabdic, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I did not say at all that the Security Council was behaving as a legislative body and that it established the International Criminal Tribunal. I only said that the Security Council adopted the Statute which established the authority of this Court, its jurisdiction and its competence to proceed to issue proceedings and to try serious grave violations of international law. These grave violations had been defined earlier in the Geneva Conventions, in The Hague Conventions and other international documents. I believe that if the Prosecutor is bringing a person before this Chamber, before this Court, then he must first establish the competence of this Court and this is part of the Statute as the procedural document. After that, he must also quote the appropriate provisions of international criminal documents. They must find the violations and see that a particular act has been defined as a crime. I never said, nor did I attack the Statute. Of course, there may be defects and objections that one could make to the Statute, but this is not our topic today. I only spoke about the Rules and, in my opinion, I think I was justified in saying that the Rules are not in agreement with international law and I would like the Trial Chamber to keep this in mind. I did not say that the Muslims attacked the Croats or the Serbs. I said that the forces of the legal state loyal to the legal existing and recognised state, the forces of a member of the United Nations, these forces loyal to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina undertook an armed intervention to remove the blockade, to free, to liberate, Konjic and to make access to and out of Konjic possible. This was the reason. The Bosnian forces, the forces loyal to the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did not attack the villages because the Serbs lived there. They attacked the villages because in these villages the population blocked the roads and shot at people, made all communication impossible. That is why they were attacked; not because they were Serbs or something else. So this is the main reason for the action that was taken by the government. Second, I must say to the Prosecutor once again that the Prosecution is evading the answer. They are dallying, they are beating about the bush. Then that is something which I think one needs to say so drastically. If the legal forces are attacking rebels, armed people, it was their duty to arrest them and to detain them. Even the witnesses for the Prosecution mentioned in the supporting material say that. The Prosecution witnesses say: "We fought for three days. We were attacking", and so on. "There were so many of us", and so on. The fact is they rose up in arms against the law and order of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is entitled to arrest and detain such people. Now we come do another question whether some mistakes were made, whether incidents occurred, but the actual detention in itself is the right, the legal right, of a State. I think that the item in the indictment which speaks about unlawful detention is wrong and unjustified. I would like to suggest that this should be resolved and shown in the pretrial procedure. There are the UN resolutions which say that Bosnia was under attack. There are reports, and we all know how the situation developed. In other words, if the Bosnian Republic had not been fighting, the question is whether anybody would be here to represent Bosnia. We would have cases like Kozarac or some other cases if it had not been for the action of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you to ask, you are really directing that in respect of count 48, which is the unlawful confinement of civilians, and also in relation to the statement in the beginning of the indictment where the so-called background is set out. Am I correct in understanding you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I think you understood me very well. I am speaking about the introduction to the indictment, the background, and the particular point in the indictment -- I do not know the number -- which speaks about the unlawful detention of civilians. This is contrary to the generally known facts. It is contrary to the decisions of the appropriate authorities of the United Nations, and so on. This introduction and this point is actually establishing a sign of coalition between bandits, on one side, and the legal government and authority, on the other hand, which is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I suppose one response to that might be: "Well, that is material that will emerge at the trial and you will be able then to deal with it". Because you are really asking us to find facts now and to rule accordingly on the facts that you put forward which, I must say, I have read about elsewhere as being necessarily so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I think this is not a matter for trial, for the trial proceedings. These are well known, generally known facts, decisions of the Security Council, decisions of the General Assembly, the findings of the various international committees. Bosnia Herzegovina had been attacked, its people had been attacked and they were entitled to defend themselves. I think this is something which is a notoriously known fact which need not be proved as the Prosecution would like us to do. I also think that it is the duty of the Court and of this Trial Chamber in this pretrial proceedings that they should examine the relation between what he says, what the Prosecutor says, the Prosecution witnesses say: "We were fighting. We attacked them. We did not allow them to pass. We did not allow them to cross". That is what the Prosecution witnesses say and this is all in the supporting material. But we all know that the State had at that time been recognised, that it existed, that it was recognised by the United Nations. Therefore, to ask us to prove that there was a state and that that state was entitled to defend itself, I think, this is absurd.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to stress once more that there are, of course, different ways to describe and different ways to interpret what happened in the underlying conflict, but we will not lose the focus of the indictment, that is, what happened in this conflict or after this conflict with people who are protected by international conventions and the crimes that are described in our Statute. So we cannot go back and establish as a fact that this happened in this way or in that way. We have to look at what happened and see if we can establish that there was an ongoing international or internal conflict, and then go on from that and focus on what happened to these protected people.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is nothing else with respect to this motion, then we will begin to hear -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Could I say -- I do not know how many times I need to repeat to the Prosecutor -- that these were not protected persons. They were people who stopped other people on the road and said: "You cannot pass". They carried weapons and they attacked other people with these weapons. They are not protected persons. Any authority, any government, is entitled to remove them. People who shoot upon a city, who prevent the supplies reaching the city, cannot be protected persons in terms of any international convention. Once they are detained, then we can speak about the extent of their protection and how they should be protected. But they are not protected at the moment when they still need to be removed and prevented from committing various acts of violence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, do you have a position regarding the out of time filing by counsel for Mr. Delic? It is styled: "Reply to Prosecutor response to Delic's motion on the form of the indictment". That was ----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No, your Honour, we do not. We accept this filing and I think I can note that many of the things said in that motion have already been debated here today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is for sure, but to the extent that it is a challenge to the jurisdiction, as I indicated, it would be out of time, unless good cause were shown. I have not heard and I have not really reviewed the reply closely enough to see whether it is even alleged good cause in terms of why was it not filed earlier. But you have not filed a response to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No, we have not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It was filed on September 26th. You have 14 days, pursuant to our standing order, to file a response to that reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think our position is that we have already responded to it. We had seen this motion beforehand and what happens now in the hindsight is, was it filed properly?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So I think we have taken care of all the facts in it already. It is already done and it is incorporated in our written response.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Karabdic, why did you not file or why did you not include in the earlier motion that you filed on the form of the indictment these positions, or why did you not file a motion challenging the subject matter jurisdiction of the Tribunal earlier than when you filed it in the reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: To be very frank, in studying the response of the Prosecutor, it was at that point that I decided that my motion, actually as submitted, was in itself not only the form of the indictment but also an objection to the jurisdiction of the Court, issued proceedings according to such an indictment. The Court cannot have the jurisdiction to work on the basis of the kind of indictment submitted by the Prosecutor. We have presented all the defects of that indictment.
