From these defects it follows that the Court has no jurisdiction to work according to this indictment. I think I filed my response on 2nd or 1st September. I did not know about your May 14th ruling. I did not know about that. So I simply submitted my response after studying the Prosecution's claim. Later, I learned that I needed approval for that. As soon as I learned about that, I actually filed a request for approval which actually should refer backwards to the motion filed earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will act on your request for leave to file this reply as soon as we can, as soon as I can look at it more carefully. We will enter an order with respect to that. Mr. Brackovic, are you ready to proceed with the motion on the form of the indictment on behalf of Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am quite ready to begin my argumentation and the verbal support to the motions that I submitted in writing. The motion contesting the form of the indictment, or rather pointing out the defects in the form of the indictment, under item 1 it says that the indictment is too general, it lacks precision, lacks definition and it is quite vague, both with regard to the nature of the offences with which my client is charged and general things such as factual description and other relevant elements which need to be indicated in the statement of facts such as time, place of the crime and all the other circumstances. I said there that the statement of facts regarding the commission of the crime and individual points contains wording such as, "Esad Landzo and others" or a group including Esad Landzo and others beat for a long time cruelly a person. Then there is also an objection regarding the wording "Esad Landzo and others". The substance of all these objection is that in view of this phraseology and description of perpetrated crimes, allegedly perpetrated by Esad Landzo, do not allow really to establish the degree of his criminal responsibility or its form. I should like to indicate a principle, that is that every person is individually responsible for acts which he or she has undertaken personally, and that such a person may not be responsible for crimes committed by other persons or for the excesses of another. In his response the Prosecutor refers to a universal legal principle, and that is that several persons may participate in the commission of a crime and each one of them may be individually charged for the crime committed. I go along with this principle. I agree that such a principle does exist. I should, nevertheless, like to supplement it by saying that every person may be responsible for offences, for crimes he or she has committed and may be held responsible only within the boundaries of his or her intent and may not be responsible for the acts perpetrated by accomplices or other participants in the crime. In response the Prosecutor refers to Article 7 of the Statute of this Tribunal which says that: "A person who planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of a crime referred to in Articles 2 to 5 of the present Statute shall be individually responsible for the crime." With regard to this provision, I should like to lay special emphasis on this part of Article 7 which says "or otherwise". The Prosecutor makes it a general provision. The Defence deems that this part of this sentence which says "or otherwise" should be interpreted in a different, in a relevant way, which means in a way which will indicate the causal relationship in an act committed by the accused when perpetrating a specific crime. May I just quote an abstract situation. For instance, if you have several persons, several individuals, participating in a crime and then, for instance, an individual perhaps slaps the person in the face, the second one pulls him by the hair, the third one hits him with a stick on the head, the fourth one uses some other instrument to beat him on the genitals and so on and so forth, and from the affects of such several attacks this person dies. The question arises whether all persons who participated in the physical ill-treatment may be held equally criminally responsible for the killing of that person, that is, whether his contribution to the commission of the crime, whether the person I indicated as the first or the second may be held responsible for the acts committed by the third or fourth person which have a direct causal relationship with the effect or rather with the death of the person subjected to this treatment. I think that there is no such causal relationship, such cause and effect, which could charge the first two individuals in this example. For instance, take another example. If several individuals participate in the battery of a person and each one of them seriously contributed to this felony. However, one of those individuals who also is participating in the beating up of that person, for instance, draws a knife and then kills that person, the question then arises whether all the persons participating in the battery of that person may be held responsible for the crime of murder. Under our criminal law theory and practice it is quite evident that not all those persons may be responsible, because the causal relationship which resulted in the death of the victim is related merely to the act of the person who drew the knife. Under our law the person who used the knife to kill the person would be charged with murder, whereas the other persons would be charged as participants in the battery which is socially unacceptable behaviour and would be tried for that, but they could not be held responsible for the killing of the victim. Therefore, I said that there must be an objective causal relationship between the act which an accused is being charged with and the effect which then follows. However, as the indictment says in the description of facts, I am afraid we cannot find the questions and find answers to them, and we cannot establish the relationship between the conduct, between the behaviour of the accused and the effect mentioned there. So the responsibility of the accused is levelled off, is equalised with the contribution or with what all the other persons who took part in these acts did. I should like also to refer to Article 47(B). Some of the counts of the indictment do not contain some of the fundamental elements relative to the place and time of commission and other circumstances which may be of relevance in this specific case. I shall also point to the evident inconsistency of the Prosecution when moving from one count to the other, as indicated by the Prosecution in their response and especially in the conclusion. The Prosecution says that all counts of the indictment contain a description of the criminal acts, time and place and probably conduct of the accused. However, I shall now go count by count and indicate. For instance, in counts 1 and 2 of the indictment which refer to the killing of Scepo Gotovac, we do not find the place of the crime. We do not know. Will your Honours read carefully this count and this count does not mention the site of the crime, whereas under other counts we find the site of the crime described. But they perhaps have the site of the crime and they lack something else which is again of relevance to a description of that particular crime. For instance, when it talks about the killing of Simo Jovanovic or Slavko Susic, these counts do not indicate the manner of commission or, sorry, Slavko Susic the site of the crime is also lacking, but on counts 7 and 8 relative to the killing of Bosko Samoukovic we do not have how the crime was committed. Counts 7 and 8 are interesting, that is again killing of Bosko Samoukovic, because the commission or rather what the accused has done is described. I am going to quote: "On that occasion Esad Landzo repeatedly struck Bosko Samoukovic aged approximately 60 years." That is the description of the manner of commission of the crime, and then it says he died soon after from his injuries. This description is inadequate, especially when such grave crimes are committed which are classified as war crimes before this International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, may I interrupt you? What is the inadequacy in counts 7 and 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: We do not see how the crime was committed. There are no details. There are no particulars regarding the manner. It only says that the accused repeatedly struck Bosko Samoukovic who died soon after from his injuries. "Several times" may mean three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What more would you want than that, the number of times he was struck or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In its response to our motion the Prosecution made it sound like a very banal motion and said that the Prosecution need not supply the exact number of blows dealt by the accused. I agree with that, that is impossible, but nevertheless there should be a description such, as for instance, we find under counts 11 and 12 relative to the killing of Slavko Susic. I think that this statement of facts meets minimal requests, the minimal standards of Rule 47(B) when it refers to a concise statement of the facts of the case. Such a statement of facts under counts 11 and 12 perhaps might be meeting the criteria standards of Tribunal. However, under counts 7 and 8 which say that the accused repeatedly struck the victim who soon after died, it makes the crime impossible because we cannot establish the causal relationship between the crime and the effect which ensued from it. It might transpire from this that the accused was a superman and that it would suffice to hit somebody several times for him to drop dead, and "several times" may be three times, not more than that. Then I said that this also relates to counts 5 and 6, that we do not see how the crime was perpetrated, how Simo Jovanovic was killed, but it is not as drastic as it appears when it comes to the case of Bosko Samoukovic. As for counts 11 and 12, I have already said that the site of the crime is not indicated. If you look carefully at this, I do not see where the crime was committed. We may make guesses about where it was, whether it was happening somewhere in outerspace or some unknown country.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: May I immediately, so we do not forget it, may I interrupt just to tell ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not want you to reply right now. Let Mr. Brackovic finish his argument. Go ahead, Mr. Brackovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: In this manner I wish to point out an inconsistency of the Prosecution. In individual counts of the indictment some principles are sometimes met, I mean the ones indicated by Rule 47(B), whereas in some other instances that particular principle is not quite met. In some counts of the indictment we have the time and the place of the crime, and then the description of the particular crime is not indicated. Sometimes we have the facts described but then not the time or the place. I think these are some of the fundamental elements which must be included in any statement of facts, especially in view of the crimes and the legal classification of these crimes. I am not familiar with the legal system of the countries from which the representatives of Prosecution come from, whether it suffices to write it like this and to charge somebody with murder. What I can say quite openly is that in my country and in other countries which emerged from the collapse of the former Yugoslavia, such statement of facts is quite inadequate and would have been returned to the Prosecution as such. This statement of facts would be inadequate even for the most ordinary crimes with plaintiffs such as light bodily injuries or verbal abuse and things like that, because they would not be meeting the principle criteria, the principle standards requested by our law and criminal proceedings. I expect that after my argumentation I will hear the response of the Prosecution to my objections and to explain these inconsistencies. I mean again that in some counts we have the site and place of the indictment. In others these are lacking. Somebody else, however, is in. Furthermore, the Defence is not asking for particulars, and the Prosecutor has not interpreted properly the substance of our motion. The Defence is asking for elementary, for basic particulars, on the basis of which one can conduct it in proper manner. That is, we are requesting a minimum and we deem that the Prosecution simply were not even up to that minimum. Furthermore, I should like to say regarding paragraph 2 of the motion that in this part I might accept the Prosecution's objection, and that the motion relevant to the form of the indictment cannot include the discussion which goes to the particular case. For this reason, I submitted no supplementary motions, or rather I did not try to supplement my motion as I had announced at a status conference on 24th July, because I realised that I would be going into the discussion of the facts and that would be the wrong way to indicate the defects in the form of the indictment. That would not be the right way to go about this. I realised that these things could be successfully discussed only in the course of the trial itself. However, one of the problems of the Defence is that after the confirmation of an indictment the Defence cannot apply for any legal procedural remedies, such as, for instance, to contest the decision of the relevant Judge or in this specific case Judge Jorda who confirmed the indictment. That is for the simple reason that there is an inaccuracy, that there is something stated inaccurately in the response to my indictment, that the killing of a certain Miljanic -- there are several witnesses talking about the killing of a certain Miljanic. I claim, however, there are not several witnesses. When I say "several" I mean at least two or more persons. The only reservation I have concerns the statements of witnesses which were redacted and which we received yesterday. They are numbers 27 to 40. For the lack of time I could not go through them. However, let this question be resolved during the trial and the Defence will endeavour to prove that there is no relevant evidence indicating the killing of a person called here a certain Miljanic. The Prosecution, however, states in its response that they have indicated the identity of each and every person. However, the identity of that person is not indicated. That person named Miljanic has both his first and last name and that is a verifiable fact. If one goes through the indictment one can see that. I should like to continue now but to pass to item 3 which is more or less of a legal nature. It says that one may be held responsible for one crime only, and that nobody can be held responsible for one crime twice as stated in the Prosecution's response. In the response it is said that there are cumulative charges, or rather that the accused is properly charged with both crimes and he may be found guilty of both crimes. I see no two crimes here. There is only one crime. If a particular person was deprived of his life and if thus only one effect took place, then we can talk about the crime of the depriving of life or murder which, however, can take place in different forms and which may be legally classified in different ways. In this specific case for the killing of one specific person or for depriving one person of life, the accused is charged twice, once for killing that person and the second time for wilful murder. In this specific case I think, without going into particulars, without discussing the facts of that particular case at issue, can we talk about the wilful killing which is a more grave offence and I think that it covers a lighter crime, that is another form of that crime which is classified as a less serious crime. This is the fundamental legal principle that nobody can be tried twice for the same criminal act. This is a universal legal principle. I would like to point out that the objections that I have raised will, of course, appear in the motions of other lawyers coming from the former Yugoslavia because our criminal law and criminal code are different. The criminal system is different from the criminal system upon which the proceedings of this Court are based. This, I think, will give rise to numerous objections and motions because we have two different legal schools at work here, and our school finds it very difficult to accept such a kind of an indictment. We as Defence lawyers would, of course, favour alternative treatment, but not cumulative treatment of crimes. This kind of description and this kind of legal qualification can be given as an alternative qualification. That would be acceptable, more acceptable than the cumulative treatment, but in view of the technology of implementation of our criminal law, even this would be difficult. It might affect the actual sentencing, the severity of the sentence, but we could never actually tolerate two crimes committed at the same time adding up, so to speak, because there is only one consequence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You know the indictment was confirmed by Judge Jorda. You mentioned that in your argument. You know that he is from the civil law system. He has his long background in France. But that should not, I suppose, make a difference because the Tribunal is not bound by national systems. So it should not change because of the Judge who confirms the indictment or the Judges who are sitting at a particular Trial Chamber. I think I understand your position, but I just wanted to mention that. We need to stand in recess for lunch now. We still have not heard the motion for provisional release for Mr. Landzo. So when we return at 2.30 we will continue in open session and complete the oral arguments on this motion, hear from the Prosecutor and you can complete yours, Mr. Brackovic. Then we will go into closed session for both the hearing on the motion for provisional release and then we had a status conference too that we wanted to continue. So we will probably have a long afternoon, but I want you to have as much time as necessary. We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Brackovic, had you completed your argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: I would need, your Honour, a few more minutes, perhaps to complete.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: I will be referring to point 4. In point 4 of the motion on the form of the indictment, the Defence states that the acts described individually and individual cases of murder or killing, since they happened in continuity and since they happened in a short period of time and that they happened in one place, that they actually represent one extended crime which is known in our legal practice. This, I think, is a universal legal institute which can apply also to this specific case, so that all these acts which are individually described and classified as individual cases of killing could, indeed, have been construed as a single act of an extended kind in view of the natural, logical and legal linkage of the acts making up this one extended act. So I think that the Prosecution is wrong when they deny the existence of an extended crime, a criminal act, but, rather, the Prosecution treats each of these acts separately as noted in the indictment. Each of them is qualified individually and would then have to be tried as individual cases. In connection with my previous objections, these objections stand also in relation to the other parts of the indictment dealing not with murder but with physical maltreatment and so on. I will note that other Defence counsel in this case did the same. Defence counsel for Mr. Mucic, for instance, Mr. Rhodes, actually asked for greater details, for more details, in the description of the acts listed in the indictment, especially focusing on the time, place and manner of the perpetration of the crime. The Prosecution says that all these details are in the accompanying supporting material with the statements of witnesses and so on which accompany the indictment, but I would like to note that this kind of terminology is unknown, especially with respect to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and with respect to the Statute. Such details would have to be in the facts of the case, and not that the Defence should go and leaf through the piles of supporting material and statements by witnesses. The Defence does not ask for unnecessary details, as the Prosecution states in their response, but, rather, we ask for a minimum. We ask for the elementary information which is the normal part and parcel of any indictment, namely, the manner of perpetration of the crime, place and time. So my objections which are listed in points 5 and 6 actually relate to the rest of the indictment dealing with torture, inflicting of physical pain and so on. In view of all this, the Defence would like to ask the Trial Chamber to accept our objections, to send the indictment back to the Prosecution for improvement for the removal of the defects or, alternatively, to reject the indictment as unordered and inapplicable in these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brackovic is also touching on the question of individual responsibility. I would like to reiterate that if a defendant is charged with criminal acts committed with others, it is never the question of responsibility for what others did; only his own acts in participation in the crime. When it comes to decide if a person taking part in a beating, for instance, leading up to the death of the victim, whether he is responsible for murder or only for the beatings, is of course a question of his intent, which in every case and in every count has to be proven by the Prosecutor. Again we have heard the indictment being criticised as vague and the facts given without exhaustive precision. When Mr. Brackovic gave examples, I could not quite follow him. It seems to me that he has overlooked what is stated in the indictment under the general allegations. For instance, the crime in count 1 and count 2 did not take place in outer space; it took place in the Celebici camp which is stated in paragraph 14 in the indictment under the heading "General Allegation" where it says: "All acts described in the paragraphs below occurred in the Celebici camp in the Konjic municipality". So the place is given for the overall indictment. No other crimes than crimes committed in the Celebici camp is in question in this indictment. The examples given, for instance, counts 7 and 8, I look at paragraph 19, and I find that the place is already given in the general allegations, the time is given, the way of mistreating the victim is given, beating him with a wooden plank. It is said that it was repeatedly done by Mr. Landzo. It says he lost consciousness from the blows and that he was taken to facilities where he died and he died from his injuries. To me, I think we by stating all these facts have given enough facts for the Defence to prepare to defend this case. I do not think we need to state more specific details than we have done just now. The Defence also again took up the question of cumulative charges which I already made some remarks about, but I just want to stress again that it is never the question of punishing a person for more than committing one criminal act in each count. This way of charging is just to show that the act in question falls under different Articles in the Statute, not ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You do not mean in each count, do you? You said not more than one act in each count -- in each paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In each paragraph. I mean in each paragraph. So it would never be the question for the Court, when coming to just judge that act, to find a person guilty or not guilty for this act in question. There was something more .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So Mr. Brackovic has said that, the way it has been charged in the indictment, this violates the accused's right not to be tried twice for the same act. It is your position that he would not be tried twice for the same act but ----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He would never be tried twice for the same act. He is tried for one act.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Murder, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then we are going to discuss under which paragraph it pleases the Court to quote when sentencing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you would not expect the Trial Chamber then to find -- if the Trial Chamber found that the accused was guilty beyond a reasonable doubt of murder, for example, and it is then alleged in count 1 in violation of the Geneva Conventions or Article 2 and count 3 -- in the next count, Article 3 etc. ----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- you would not expect the Trial Chamber then to find that the accused has violated both laws, but only one of them, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I could just fancy the Court saying: "He committed this act" and then, as it is done in my jurisdiction in Sweden, for instance, it happens that the Court quotes all these different laws or paragraphs under which this behaviour falls, but always keeping in mind that he is not convicted for having committed more than this one crime. Then they give it a name, for instance, murder and can say then it falls also under this and that prohibition, but gives sentencing just for committing one thing, namely, murder.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Brackovic says that this would affect, though, the severity of the sentence if the Trial Chamber were to find that he violated both Article 2 of our Statute as well as Article 3, for example -- no, Article 5, that might be a better choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It could be for the Prosecutor to argue the graveness, pointing out that he has been violating more than one of the Articles in the Statute, but I think the Prosecutor has to decide whether he, in the first hand, proposes that he is going to be sentenced. I will go on with only one more thing ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why are they not charged alternatively then? Why not? Mr. Brackovic said that it would be less egregious if it was alternative, not that that would please him, but it would be better than cumulative. Why not then charge alternatively, since you do not expect the Trial Chamber to sentence except on one count?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When I first arrived at this Tribunal, I was very surprised by the way of charging. In my jurisdiction, the Prosecutor would choose for what crime to charge and not do this cumulatively, as I know they do in, for instance, the American jurisdiction. I would in Sweden have decided to say he committed this crime. Then I can point out to the Court that he has by doing so also violated other prohibitions in the legal system or in the penal code. But he would never, to my experience, be sentenced for more than one thing, the main thing, that the Court chooses that this is, and then they could quote even in their judgment the other prohibitions which have been violated. I do not think, to come back to your first question, that there is this one act to be judged and ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You say you do not think or you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: My argument was that I just -- I did not quite follow your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry. There is one act to be judged, murder, for example ----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- and you say that it could violate a number of Articles ----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- and that it should be taken into consideration only at sentencing. But then you also say that the Trial Chamber could find that he had violated the other Articles as well, but in any case you do agree, though, that there would be one act?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Never more than one act. Then I just have one other thing to take up what the Defence lawyer said in his final arguments. I understand he would like to see many of the crimes in counts 1 and 2 -- they are enumerated in his written motion -- to be charged as one extended criminal act. My answer to that is: maybe that it could have been possible to charge in such a fashion. However, the Prosecutor has chosen to charge them as separate acts against individual victims which, in my opinion, it also is. To do so, to choose in what way to charge, lies, in my opinion, in the Prosecutor's discretion and all the counts have been so confirmed. Yes, I think that is what I deem necessary to say in answer to the Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Brackovic? Do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to say something in connection with what we heard by the Prosecution. By saying what he said, the Prosecutor actually has recognised the justification of my objection with regard to the cumulative charges. I read in the Bosnian version -- I can read the English version as well, if you like, which refers to what the Prosecutor said. The Prosecutor says on page 5 in section (C) in the second paragraph: "The accused is properly charged with both crimes, and he may be found guilty on both charges". What the Prosecutor has just said goes counter to what he says in the response to the Defence motion in connection with the cumulation of charges, because I think the Defence is just claiming that nobody can be charged twice or accused twice for the same criminal act. In the answer, in fact, in the response, the Prosecution says that the accused can be found guilty of both charges, although this is only one crime, one criminal act, which can be qualified legally in different ways. This is a matter of nuance very often. Once we have an act of killing which can be treated as the basic form of crime, depriving a victim of his or her life, but at the same time the accused is charged also with wilful killing or wilful murder. The Prosecutor will have to decide which of these two qualifications he would endorse. I said earlier that the reason why we have this disagreement is the different technology of the presentation of the indictment. This probably comes due to the different legal systems of the Defence and of the Prosecution. If we relied on alternative statements, that might be better perhaps. But, obviously, the Trial Chamber is not bound by the qualification of the case, legal qualification of the case, but by the facts, description of the facts. So the important thing is that we have the facts right and the legal qualification is only secondary, at least in our system of law. Let me also say in connection with what the Prosecutor has said, referring to the place of the criminal act, the place is not described, although in point 14, paragraph 14, it says that all of these acts took place in Celebici camp in the Konjic municipality. But earlier I made a digression. My intention was not to try to belittle the Prosecutor's work. I respect the Prosecution and also the Prosecutors and Prosecution counsel is present here. But I was referring to Rule 47(B) which says that the indictment will specify the "name and particulars of the suspect, and a concise statement of the facts of the case and of the crime with which the suspect is charged". The place is described in general terms. The action did, indeed, take place in the Celebici camp, but when it comes to describing the actual place of crime, this is not given. I would like to show some other parts of the indictment where the place is, indeed, described. For instance, in counts 5 and 6, dealing with Simo Jovanovic's killing, it says it was in front of the building. Then in Nos. 9 and 10 they say that he entered into a detention building. So that means sometimes it is a detention facility, sometimes outside the detention facilities, so we do have a description of place. But in counts 7 and 8, having to do with the killing of Bosko Samoukovic -- sorry, I apologise, this is wrong. I am speaking about counts 11 and 12 and the killing of Slavko Susic, there we do not know which was the place of the crime. So I was, in fact, comparing different treatment and different counts so that I am trying to show the inconsistency of the Prosecution. We cannot understand why in some counts the place of the crime is very clearly described, while in some other counts this has been left out or not given. In fact, I think what we need is a kind of universal principle. The universal principle that the Court should uphold is that there must be always present the basic element, the place, time and concise description of the actions performed in the criminal act. This had to do, particularly, with the description of the act of crime. In my earlier statement and argument, I said that in some of the counts we do find that the action is described. In counts numbered 9 and 10 it says he used a baseball bat to beat the detainee to death. This is the minimum requirement on the part of the Defence, as far as the manner of the perpetration of the act is concerned. In 11 and 12, for instance, having to do with the killing of Slavko Susic, where it is said that the accused together with others tortured him using pliers, lit fuses and nails; and after being subjected to this treatment for several days, Slavko Susic died from his injuries. If we took this as a paragon, as a model, for the description of the manner of action and the manner of performance of the criminal act, we will find that in some other counts such description is lacking. In counts 7 and 8, having to do with the killing of Bosko Samoukovic, it is simply not enough under any criteria to simply state that the accused repeatedly struck Bosko Samoukovic and then Bosko Samoukovic died as a result of this. This kind of description, describing just several blows, makes us suspicious. The question is whether we can say that there is a causal relationship between such actions and such outcome. Therefore, the Defence asks for a more specific description without going into unnecessary details. I would say we do not ask for the exact number of blows and so on -- of course, this is impossible -- but when it comes to the means with which the action is performed, the Prosecutor had to state in what way, with what means, a particular person was killed. For this reason, the Defence suggests that the Prosecution should be asked to order, revise the indictment in such a way as to satisfy the elementary requirements for such a document. We do not ask for any special details, but we do ask a minimum below which we cannot accept the indictment. Also, we do not accept the Prosecution explanation that the Defence should be sent to go to the supporting materials. Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg? Do you have anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just maybe one thing: where lies the balance between necessary details and a concise statement of the facts, we must find somewhere to do this. We can go on when you prepare an indictment to state all details and facts in a description of an act; you can also find some middle way of doing it. I think this middle way found by the Prosecutor's Office in this respect meets the requirements of Article 18 and Rule 47. So, I think we feel ourselves on firm ground when we give facts like these I took as examples from the indictment. I think we have given concise facts and then we could, of course, have put in more details, but these details can easily be found in the supporting material. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Brackovic, do you have a last word, a final last word?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: There is always something that the Defence can add -­ you are right -- but I had something in mind and I forgot it, so let me use this opportunity to say this. The Prosecution in an earlier response said that there should be intent, the intent in the act of killing and so on. I share the Prosecution's view. However, that intent must be mentioned, must be demonstrated and must stem or derive from the facts. From the description of the facts, the intention to kill somebody. From the facts and from the manner of execution, we must be able to deduce that that was present, that the intent was indeed present. In this way, we would avoid the principle of collective responsibility or the collective accountability or the responsibility by the objective situation, so that the accused might have just found himself in a group of people performing such an act. So the intention needs to be stated, needs to be described, and it must logically derive from the actions made and taken by the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Brackovic, just one question, and that is what is the relationship of Article 21.4(A) to this issue? Article 21 in the Statute of the Tribunal is entitled "Rights of the accused", and 4 says: "In the determination of any charge against the accused, pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality: (A) to be informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands of the nature and cause of the charge against him". In your opinion, does that relate to the indictment, nature and cause of the charge against him? Then, of course, 18.4 deals with the responsibility of the Prosecutor and what must be done by the Office to prepare an indictment. Does the indictment, this present indictment, inform the accused of the nature and cause of the charge against him or do you think that Article, Article 21.4(A), does not apply to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRACKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this Article is, in fact, involved and it has to be linked with Article 21(A) and 18.4. Article 21, para. 4(A), the indictment must meet the requirements of Article 18.4, to have the facts and the description of the crime and so on. So that once this is done properly, then the accused can, in fact, be informed about the detail, the nature and cause of the charge against him, because this does not derive from the legal qualifications but from the facts and the description of the actions taken, performed, by the accused. The accused is not a lawyer but, as a person who is legally ignorant, will of course understand the facts of the case, but he need not necessarily understand the legal qualification of the charges. So that the accused can understand the nature and cause of the charge against him, it is very necessary that this description, the facts, should be presented and described in such a way that the accused can unambiguously understand the nature and cause of the charges against him. Your question, I think, is very relevant because in this case and in this way, the way the indictment stands now, the accused cannot be considered, informed, about the nature and cause of the charge to the extent that the description of the facts of the case does not have all the details about the place, time and manner of the criminal act. When it comes to the place of the criminal act, the place ought to be described in such a way that it can be specifically identified in a micro-locality. Are we talking about in front of a hangar? In front of the detention facility? In the tunnel? Outside the tunnel? These are the kinds of requirements pertaining to the place of the criminal act. The place must be described in such a way that it can be unmistakably determined, not simply say that it is the Celebici camp. The Celebici camp is too large. The exact place and location of the crime is very relevant also for the Defence before this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostberg, do you have a burning -- I do not know how many times we have gone back and forth now, I have forgotten, but in any case we will now go into closed session and hear the motion that will be submitted by Mr. Brackovic. Then we will continue to be in closed session for the status conference. So we will stand in recess for 10 minutes in order to convert this to a closed session.

procedural_notes.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time)
